heading: 1a. What your 10kKO leaves have in common
question: Do Diagrams 1 to 7 show what you mean by 10kKO? And what should the checker print on your 10kKO leaves where one side's capture is already a real threat, such as the first leaf of 13547 in Diagrams 13 to 17?

options.label: 10kKO
options.meaning: Keep your label. besogo grades 10kKO like an approach ko in which the attacker needs one approach, so in this KILL problem like A-1KO- and A-1KO+ alike, and no grading changes. But by your definitions this is an approach ko, not a 10kKO: White's capture threatens from the start (Diagram 14), so White can win by winning the ko at any time.

options.label: A-1KO-
options.meaning: Your approach ko: White takes first, and Black needs one approach and two threats more than White, as A-1KO- implies (Diagrams 13 to 17). besogo counts 10kKO equal to both A-1KO- and A-1KO+, but ranks A-1KO+ higher for Black, and the tree writes A-1KO+ on the neighbouring leaves. So writing A-1KO- on this leaf alone makes Black's A14 wrong at moves 11 and 13, and the problem's own status, which besogo takes from its best leaf, becomes A-1KO+.

options.label: A-1KO+
options.meaning: The tree's label for the same kind of approach ko at the next leaf (Diagrams 18 and 19). besogo grades it like 10kKO, so no move's grading changes; only the problem's own status becomes A-1KO+. But in besogo it says that Black takes first, which implies one threat more for Black; here White takes first and Black needs two.

recommendation: Yes to 10kKO for the shape of Diagrams 1 to 7, and for 10393 (Diagrams 8 to 12), whose extra White move costs nothing. On the leaves where one side's capture already threatens, the approach form your definition gives: A-1KO- on the first leaf of 13547. The checker should report your 10kKO there as notation, not as an error, wherever besogo counts the two labels equal, as on 13547; rewriting the tree is your choice, and on 13547 it changes the grading of Black's A14, because of the A-1KO+ leaves next to it.
text: Your answer describes three cases. In an approach ko one side's capture already threatens, and only the other side must approach first. In 10kKO one side must make an investment that is wasted, whoever started. In the symmetric case, shown in part 1b, both sides need an approach and the ko switches there and back; you would call that a plain KO. Below, your 27 10kKO leaves are sorted by these definitions.

Diagrams 1 to 7 show the shape your clearest 10kKO leaves share (problem 10391): each side's capture needs the same one move at a shared liberty, and whoever plays it, the other side then captures for free and holds a direct ko. That is your 10kKO exactly. It cannot switch back, so it is not the symmetric case. The table lists three more leaves with this shape, and a fourth where White, the defender, is the side that needs the ko.

Diagrams 8 to 12 (problem 10393) have no ko on the board yet: White must make it, and White needs one move more than Black before its capture threatens. These moves cost White nothing in the count, so the leaf behaves like Diagrams 1 to 7. The table has one more leaf where one side needs an extra move, in 13549: there the ko is already on the board, the extra move is Black's, and the count is still one, as in Diagrams 1 to 7.

Diagrams 13 to 17 (problem 13547) show an approach ko by your own definition: White's capture threatens from the start, and only Black needs an approach. Diagrams 18 and 19 show the next leaf of the same tree, the same kind of approach ko with the same count, written A-1KO+. The table lists seven such leaves, five more where White's capture already threatens, seven the searches cannot decide, and one with no ko.

A correction to our question 1: it named 10408 as a leaf where each side's capture needs one approach, but Diagram 20 shows that White's capture there is a real threat at once. Part 1b corrects what we said about 10403, 9883 and 7487.

How to read the checks: when a side must pass, the other side gets free moves. A capture that wins with one free move is a real threat; a capture that needs two must first add a move, an approach or an investment. Every check searches the checker's own area. A wider area gives the same results for 10391, and for 10393 whenever a side must pass, but leaves several checks of 10393 and 13547, and both of 10408's, undecided.

positions.heading: Problem 10391, leaf 4: the shape of your clearest 10kKO leaves
text: Black kills. White's group and Black's corner stones share the liberties a and b, and only Black needs the ko: without it, White lives (Diagram 1). After either side's capture the other side's stones still have a and b, so neither capture threatens anything until its side adds a move there (Diagrams 2 and 3). That move is the investment, and Diagrams 4 to 7 show that it is wasted whoever plays it.

positions.heading: Problem 10393, leaf 1: no ko on the board yet
text: Black lives. There is no ko yet: White must make one by playing at A19, which puts Black 3 in atari. Black's group and White's corner stones share a and b, as in Diagrams 1 to 7, and Black's group has one more liberty at c. So after White takes, Black still has a, b and c, and after Black retakes, White still has a and b.

positions.heading: Problem 13547, leaf 1: an approach ko written 10kKO
text: Black kills. White can take the ko at once, and White's capture always threatens: in your words, White can win by winning one ko at any time. Black's retake leaves White's stones with the liberties a and b, so Black must fill one of them before its capture threatens. That is your approach ko, and Black needs two threats more than White, as A-1KO- implies.
